subject: sociology
title: Methods in Context: Methods for Family & Crime
welcome_lead: Sensitive topics demand different methods — and different ethics.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology methods in context family crime sensitive topics.
final_note: Method must fit the topic, the people and the ethics.

concepts.def: Topic causing distress/risk — requires gentler methods.
Participants recruit peers — useful for hidden populations.
Researcher hides identity — high validity, ethical risk.

walkthroughs.body_html: Families are private spaces. Hochschild (1989) 'Second Shift': observational + interview study of dual-earner couples found women did extra unpaid hours. Sensitive topics (abuse, divorce) need rapport and confidentiality. Oakley (1981): feminist methodology — interviews as conversation.

Crime is often hidden; victims and offenders may distrust researchers. Official crime stats miss the dark figure. Self-report studies ask offenders directly — Junger-Tas reported European-wide juvenile self-report data. Victim surveys like the CSEW capture unreported crime. Covert observation: Patrick (1973) joined a Glasgow gang.

No single method covers everything. Triangulation uses multiple methods to cross-check — Hochschild combined interviews and observation. Mixed methods are now standard in sociology. The BSA Code requires informed consent, anonymity, avoiding harm and honesty about results.
